analysis.one_liner: Makes petroleum spills eligible for Superfund cleanup and polluter liability.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees from July 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021, with just 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, petroleum is carved out of the Superfund program, the federal system that makes polluters pay to clean up contaminated sites. This bill would remove that carve-out, so oil and fuel spills — including landlocked leaks that other pollution laws may not reach — could trigger Superfund cleanup and liability for the companies responsible. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near contaminated sites — leaking fuel tanks, sludge pits, and oil dumps — would gain a federal path to cleanup funded first by the responsible companies rather than left unabated or paid by local taxpayers [S2]. Communities whose groundwater is fouled by fuel leaks would be able to have the release treated as a Superfund matter, with the polluter-payer liability and cleanup machinery of the program applied to it [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds petroleum products to the legal definition of hazardous substances under Superfund (CERCLA), so a fuel or oil release can be treated like any other hazardous-contamination cleanup, with liability falling on those responsible [S2] [S3].

Closes a gap for landlocked spills: a petroleum release counts as a Superfund release when any other federal law establishes liability, targeting leaks onto land and groundwater that today fall between the cracks of federal cleanup programs [S2] [S3].
Defines petroleum product broadly — including fuel oil, sludge, and oil refuse mixed with wastes — so companies cannot reclassify oily waste as something outside the law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, fuel distributors, and owners of tanks and facilities where petroleum is released would bear the cost of Superfund-style cleanups and liability that the petroleum exclusion currently shields them from [S2] [S3]. Some of those costs could be passed through to consumers in fuel prices, and small operators with old storage tanks could face cleanup bills for legacy leaks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and fuel companies and tank owners

drawbacks.text: Superfund liability is strict and reaches many parties who handled a contaminant, so adding petroleum could pull small fuel dealers, independent gas stations, and owners of aging storage tanks into costly cleanup and litigation over old leaks [S3].

A broad definition covering 'petroleum or oil of any kind, in any form' increases the scope of potential exposure across the fuel supply chain, and some of those compliance and cleanup costs would likely be passed to consumers at the pump [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living with fuel-contaminated land and groundwater, the bill offered a real remedy: it would put cleanup costs on the companies that caused the pollution instead of leaving sites untended. The main cost is expanded liability that could reach small fuel handlers as well as major oil companies, and modest price pass-through. The design — limiting the new trigger to releases already covered by other federal law — was an attempt to target genuine gaps rather than every minor spill. On balance the bill's benefits ran to the public and its costs to industry, which is exactly why it faced an uphill path in a Congress that never took it up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their subcommittees, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on July 26, 2019, joined by three Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Sewell, Connolly, and Grijalva [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Speaker referred it to two committees with jurisdiction — Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure — meaning it had to clear both panels to advance [S1] [S5].

Three days later it was sent to subcommittees in each committee, the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee, where it remained with no hearings, markups, or further action through the end of the Congress [S5].
With only 3 cosponsors in a 431-seat House and no committee action in 17 months, the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies, fuel distributors, and storage-tank owners are better off: they keep the existing exemption of petroleum from Superfund liability and cleanup obligations, leaving contaminated sites to be addressed under narrower programs or not at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies and tank owners

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend Superfund liability to petroleum releases

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition is recorded; all four sponsors were Democrats, but the bill died in committee without any recorded position from either party.

industries.note: The bill would end petroleum's exemption from Superfund, exposing oil companies to cleanup liability and costs for fuel and oil spills, including leaks onto land and groundwater. Its interest in keeping that exemption runs directly against residents of contaminated communities.

Gas stations, fuel terminals, and tank farms with leaking underground storage tanks would face Superfund-style cleanup liability for spills the current exclusion shields them from. Because Superfund liability reaches many parties in the chain of handling, smaller operators could be swept in alongside major companies.
